title: Parallel query processing
lead: Shared-resource architectures, data placement, parallel operators and distributed join plans.

sections.title: Architectures and levels of parallelism
sections.html:
Resources and parallel database goals

Parallel/distributed execution spreads work over CPU, memory, storage and network while preserving one logical query result. Nearby parallel nodes assume faster communication than widely distributed nodes, but communication is still a resource. Architecture specifies which resources processors can directly share and therefore where coordination and data movement are required.

PDF pp. 1–4

Shared memory, shared disk, shared nothing

Shared memory gives CPUs one address space and fast communication, with synchronization and interconnect limits. Shared disk gives each processor private memory and access to common persistent storage; execution and storage can scale separately, but caches/locks still require coordination and the shared storage can bottleneck. One data copy does not automatically solve concurrent-cache consistency or make the disk failure-proof.

Shared nothing gives each instance its own CPU, memory and disk, typically on commodity nodes. Capacity grows by adding nodes, but remote data access and consistent updates require network protocols. These are resource-sharing architectures; a real deployment can combine levels of them.

PDF pp. 5–8

The three levels of parallel execution

Inter-query parallelism runs different queries concurrently and needs concurrency control. Intra-query parallelism divides one query. Its inter-operator form overlaps pipeline stages, or runs independent branches of a bushy tree; materialisation barriers delay dependent stages. Its intra-operator form partitions a scan, sort or join across workers. These dimensions can coexist, so extra workers for one query can compete with other users for the same resources.

PDF pp. 9–11

sections.title: Partitioning and replication
sections.html:
Horizontal partitioning and routing

Horizontal partitions are disjoint row subsets, each row retaining all columns. Round-robin places rows 101…105 on P1,P2,P3,P4,P1, spreading counts but offering no value-based pruning. The source hash example places a,b,c,d,e on P2,P4,P3,P2,P1 using the selected key’s hash modulo four. An equality lookup can route directly; grouping and equijoins can benefit from colocated keys.

Range placement uses [a,c],[d,e],[f,m],[n,z]: a,b,c go to P1 and d,e to P2. It supports equality/range pruning, but skewed values or accesses can overload a range. A partition key should consider bytes, access load and usage, not just equal tuple counts.

PDF pp. 12–16

Replication and data transparency

Partition replication stores additional copies of a partition; table replication places an entire table at multiple locations, often for a small read-mostly dimension. Updates must propagate according to the system’s consistency protocol; copying does not itself specify synchronous or eventual visibility.

Applications should use the same logical tables without manually locating shards or replicas. The DBMS translates the query into fragments and combines results with the promised semantics. Replicas represent the same logical rows and must not multiply query results.

PDF pp. 17–19

sections.title: Parallel scans, hashing and sorting
sections.html:
Parallel scans and key lookup

Using decimal units, 100 TB / 0.5 GB/s = 200,000 seconds ≈2.31 days. An ideal 100-worker division gives 2,000 seconds ≈33 minutes. This assumes balanced independent storage bandwidth and negligible extra overhead; a shared bottleneck or skew prevents ideal speedup.

Concatenate disjoint scan outputs, then perform any required global operation. A predicate can skip nodes excluded by a range/hash partition rule. A lookup on the partition key routes to the relevant node; without applicable location information it may need broadcast. A local index alone does not identify which remote node holds the key.

PDF pp. 20–21

Parallel hashing and hash join

Use hn to assign tuples to network nodes, then local hp to partition external data and hr for an in-memory hash table. Keep these functions’ roles distinct. For a hash join, repartition both inputs with the same join-key function so every matching pair meets on one node; perform ordinary local Grace/hash joins there. Equal keys must go to the same destination, including duplicate-key groups. Network partitioning does not guarantee a local build partition fits memory.

PDF pp. 22–23

Parallel sorting and sort-merge join

Range-partition input, externally sort each machine’s range and concatenate outputs in range order for a global ordering. Hash-partitioned sorted pieces do not form global order by simple concatenation. For sort-merge join, use identical join-key ranges on both inputs, then locally sort and merge each pair. Range boundaries and equal boundary keys must be assigned consistently, or matches can be lost. The general requirement is to colocate matching rows without collecting entire large tables onto one machine.

PDF pp. 24–26

sections.title: Four distributed join layouts
sections.html:
Join scenario one: a replicated input

R is disjointly partitioned by id (1…100 on one node,101…200 on another); S is fully replicated. Each node joins its own R fragment with one local S copy, then the coordinator combines results. Each logical R row participates at one owner, so S replication does not duplicate answers. No join-input network shuffle is needed, though result gathering and maintaining S replicas still cost work.

PDF pp. 27–28

Join scenario two: compatible partitioning

Both tables use compatible id boundaries and placement: the node holding R ids 1…100 also holds S ids 1…100. Local joins cover every possible match, and results can be combined. Merely saying “both are partitioned” is insufficient: the join keys, mapping and destination ownership must align.

PDF pp. 29–30

Join scenario three: broadcast the small table

R is partitioned by id, while S is partitioned by val. If S is small, gather/distribute all its fragments so each R owner receives the full S, then execute local joins and combine results. The animation shows the transfer, completed copies, joins and gathered answer. Broadcasting n-byte S to p workers costs on the order of (p−1)n network bytes in a simple model; small is relative to network, memory and concurrency, not a fixed row threshold.

PDF pp. 31–35

Join scenario four: repartition both inputs

R initially uses name ranges A–M,N–Z and S uses val ranges 1–50,51–100; neither places id matches together. Redistribute R by id, then S with the same id mapping, execute corresponding local joins and combine. The staged drawings show R movement, completed R partitioning, S movement, completed S partitioning, local computation and output.

Every input row must have a destination that agrees across both relations. Repartitioning moves much of R+S but preserves parallel local work; centralising both tables would concentrate network traffic, memory and computation at one node.

PDF pp. 36–42

sections.title: Network cost and skew
sections.html:
Planning for network cost and the slowest worker

Predicate pushdown, early projection and join ordering still help, now also by reducing transmitted bytes. The optimiser must track partitioning, replication, placement and ordering as physical properties, and cost exchanges and synchronization as well as local work.

For parallel branches taking 500 ms and 300 ms, the stage cannot complete before 500 ms, not their average 400 ms. Total query time follows its critical path plus exchanges; sum of I/Os across machines measures a different resource. Skew can leave one worker dominating while others idle. Architecture, query execution, concurrency control and recovery all become harder when coordination crosses resources.

PDF pp. 43–45

quiz.question: Workers take 4, 5, 5, and 15 seconds in one parallel phase. What is the lower bound on the phase duration?
quiz.explanation: The phase must wait for its slowest worker. Coordination and network overhead may increase the total duration further.

source.summary: Lecture 26 compares resource-sharing architectures, levels of parallelism, partitioning and replication, parallel scans, sorts, and joins, and cost models that account for network traffic and skew.
